parts:
For starters, you really should consider weaning yourself of qplot. If you have complex plots that require more than a few adjustments then it's best to spell everything out with ggplot() adding a layer at a time. In my mind, it's easier to keep track of what you're doing. 

ggplot()+

geom_point(data=df, aes(x=ventilation, y=folate), position=position_jitter(w=0.1, h=0.1))+

geom_point(data=mydata, aes(x=ventilation, y=mymean),shape=4,size=5)+

geom_line(data=mydata, aes(x=ventilation, y=mymean, group=1))+

geom_errorbar(data=mydata, aes(x=ventilation, y=mymean, ymin=min, ymax=max), width=0.1)

For the line to connect, you need group=1 to indicate that they all connect. When you told it to assume the points were numeric it did something similar. I've never used as.numeric to get around this and I'm surprised it worked, but it worked so that's great, but I wouldn't assume it will work in every case. 

The reason your errorbars weren't plotting was because you didn't specify a "y", so I'm assuming that it didn't know where to put them. If you got an error from it, it would have been helpful if you had put that into your email. 

Also, if you could use dput() to output your data it would be a lot easier for us to get right to your example. Plus, it's easy.

dput(red.cell.folate)

Brandon

There are enough examples in the book. Your situation is covered, but
not in the context of your particular problem - all the pieces are
discussed in various sections of the book, including group = 1 (see p.
51). Another source of help is the set of on-line help pages:
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/

Scroll down towards the bottom of the page and you'll find individual
help pages for each of the major groups of functions in ggplot2;
within the help of each function are a series of examples with
attached plots to show the effect of the code. The major omission in
this set of help pages concerns opts() [Chapter 8 of the book].
Brandon collected a set of examples last year and built the following
page on the ggplot2 wiki to cover that swath of material:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/%2Bopts%28%29-List

If you go to its parent page, https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki,
you'll find more information about ggplot2, including several sets of
extended examples, most of which use more advanced features of the
package. It's not mentioned in the book because it was created after
the book was published.

Finally, I often search the archives of this list to glean
information. Many common situations have been discussed before,
including this one and the parallel situation of dodged box plots with
jittered points. It's fair to warn you that most of the helpers on
this list use ggplot() rather than qplot(), but most of the time the
translation is straightforward. ggplot() requires a data frame input,
but qplot() is somewhat more forgiving - e.g., it will accept atomic
vectors as input. For the most part, qplot() is more 'automatic'
whereas ggplot() provides the user with more control, but for 95% or
so of the plots one would normally make, either way will work. One
could also make the argument that qplot() syntax is easier to
understand.

The key to the system is to learn the roles of layers, geoms, scales,
facets, coordinate systems, etc. and to realize that plots can be
constructed in a modular fashion, which can sometimes mean that the
order in which certain elements appear can matter in the rendered
plot. In the end, all of the pieces are integrated and need to
coordinate. That last part, the coordination, takes some time to
figure out. As Hamlet would say, 'Ay, there's the rub.'

>
> the Parameter "group" only show two times in his book, so I still dont
> know if you dont specify it, what is the default value of "group". I
> am still confused

Most of the time, you only need to worry about group when you want to
make a plot that connects across different levels of a factor. More
specifically, geom_line() expects that the 'x' is numeric - when it's
not, the line won't be plotted. The group construct helps you get
around this limitation. If only one line is needed across factor
categories, then adding group = 1 to the aes() argument works; if you
need multiple lines to be connected across levels of a horizontal axis
factor (let's call it A) for each level of another factor (say B),
then you should use group = B in aes(). The spaghetti plot example on
pp. 50-51 of the ggplot2 book illustrates both uses with the Orthodont
data.

>
> thanks for the dput function,
>
> another question,
>
>  how to convert the output of dput back to data.frame?

No conversion is needed - just assign a name, copy and paste it to
your R session and you're done. structure() is an R function that
outputs the contents and structure of an R object. It's particularly
useful when passing data from your R session to e-mail because it
retains the class and attribute structure of the (data) object, which
is not necessarily the case when you copy and paste the data itself
from your R session. For example, it's not obvious in your copied data
whether the ventilation variable is character or factor - I could read
it in either way. dput() removes the ambiguity: from the output below,
you have ventilation as a factor variable. Case closed - ambiguity
resolved. Dates and other types of objects can also be in a data frame
and once again dput() clarifies structure. I've seen examples where
dput() indicated that certain parts of a data frame were matrices or
lists, which would never have been recognized by copy and paste. This
is often meaningful when trying to resolve problems that arise in
programming.

To see what I mean, open a fresh R session and do this:

red.cell.folate <- [ now copy and paste the dput() output from your
last e-mail (without R prompts/continuation chars) ]
str(red.cell.folate)
red.cell.folate

Then compare the result of this str() with a similar str() in the
other session from which you created the dput() - they should be
identical. This is how a receiver can be guaranteed that his/her
version of your data matches yours, which makes it easier to resolve
problems remotely.

As for your problem, here's a way to do it using qplot() and an
alternative way using ggplot() that differs only in detail from
Brandon's code - since most of the elements can be extracted from a
summary data frame, I use it as the default in ggplot().

# qplot() method:
qplot(ventilation, folate, data = red.cell.folate, geom = 'jitter') +
stat_summary(fun.y = mean, colour = 'blue', geom = 'line', aes(group = 1)) +
stat_summary(fun.y = mean, colour = 'blue', geom = 'point', size = 3) +
stat_summary(fun.data = 'mean_sdl', mult = 1, geom = 'errorbar',
colour = 'blue', width = 0.3)

### Cons:
## (1) can only use one data frame (as far as I know, but I could be
wrong), so needs
## to use stat_summary() to plot the summary pieces.
## (2) can't control the amount of jitter in the strip plots - geom_jitter
## doesn't take a position_jitter argument that allows for jitter control,

## ggplot() method:
# Another way to get the summary info by factor level:
rcfsumm <- ddply(red.cell.folate, .(ventilation), summarise,
mean = mean(folate), sd = sd(folate))

# Using the summary data frame as input for all but the points below:
ggplot(rcfsumm, aes(x = ventilation, y = mean)) +
geom_point(data = red.cell.folate, aes(x = ventilation, y = folate),
position = position_jitter(width = 0.1)) +
geom_point(size = 3, colour = 'blue') +
geom_line(aes(group = 1), colour = 'blue') +
geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ventilation, xmax = ventilation,
ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd),
colour = 'blue', width = 0.3)

## Cons:
#### * requires data frame input
#### * more code
#### * more specific code
## Pros:
#### * allows different geoms to access different data frames
#### * => less dependence on stat_summary() to do the right thing
#### * gives one more control over the amount of jitter, since
#### geom_point() can take a position argument equal to
#### position_jitter; the latter function has width and height arguments
#### that provide finer control.

Except for the amount of jitter (which would matter to me), the two
plots should be the same.

BTW, I found the mean_sdl() function at the on-line help page for
stat_summary().

HTH,
